item.title: Disturbance heading toward Marianas could develop into a tropical storm or typhoon
item.description: Forecasters are watching Invest 96W, a disturbance near Kosrae that could develop into a tropical storm or typhoon as it heads toward the Marianas. But the system’s track, timing and intensity are highly uncertain.
item.content:encoded:
Forecasters are watching Invest 96W, a disturbance near Kosrae that could develop into a tropical storm or typhoon as it heads toward the Marianas.

But the system’s track, timing and intensity are highly uncertain.

The system will continue to organize as it begins moving west-northwest toward the Marianas over the next few days, according to the National Weather Service.

It could pass anywhere from south of Guam to Alamagan in the far northern CNMI, likely sometime this upcoming weekend.

Forecasters are advising residents in the Marianas to maintain a general state of preparedness for the possibility of a passing tropical cyclone.

Meanwhile, Tropical Depression 28W with maximum sustained winds of 35 mph is expected to track to the northwest over the next few days, passing through the far northern CNMI near Agrihan as a tropical depression Tuesday night.

item.content:encoded:
Shriners Children’s Hawaii and its Honolulu medical outreach team are returning to Guam Oct. 26-30 to provide free medical consultations for youth, according to the Department of Public Health and Social Services.

The Honolulu medical outreach team will be providing free medical consultations for children up to 17 years old with orthopedic conditions, healed burns, or sports injuries at the Northern Region Community Health Center in Dededo.

The Shriner's team was scheduled to assist in Guam in July, but the clinic was canceled due to Typhoon Bavi. Public Health is bringing the Honolulu team back to assist with the clinical backlog from the disaster.

For new patients, applications may be picked up at the Northern Region Community Health Center in Dededo, Room 30, Monday through Friday, 8:30 a.m. to 11 a.m. and from 1:30 p.m. to 4 p.m.

Parents and guardians may also request to receive the application by emailing DPHSS’s Medical Social Services staff, Cherisse Santiago at cherisse.santiago@dphss.guam.gov or Nicole Loren-Duplito at nicole.lored@dphss.guam.gov

Applicants must submit the completed application along with their child’s birth certificate, a parent identification card, and proof of legal guardianship, if applicable. A physician referral is not required, and Public Health says self-referrals are welcome.

For more information about upcoming on-island outreach clinics or to schedule a telehealth consultation, contact the Medical Social Services staff via email or call 671-634-7408.

item.title: CNMI seeks federal support for $12.5B in infrastructure projects
item.description: The Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands has submitted more than $12.5 billion in infrastructure project profiles for federal consideration following last month’s Interagency Regional Convening in San Francisco, officials said. item.content:encoded:
The Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands has submitted more than $12.5 billion in infrastructure project profiles for federal consideration following last month’s Interagency Regional Convening in San Francisco, officials said.

Special Assistant for Military Affairs Edward C. Camacho said the figure reflects the value of proposed projects—not approved funding—and stressed that federal agencies urged the CNMI to focus on initiatives that strengthen both civilian services and U.S. defense readiness.

“We were asking for a rescue, and they were listening,” Camacho said.

The CNMI’s submissions span power generation, water security, seaports, airports, healthcare facilities, and roads. Officials told federal partners that aging systems, storm damage, geographic isolation, and limited local revenue make it increasingly difficult to maintain essential services.

The convening, hosted by the Department of War’s Office of Local Defense Community Cooperation, brought CNMI and Guam officials together with multiple federal agencies to discuss how civilian infrastructure investments could align with national security requirements in the Western Pacific.

Gov. David M. Apatang, who remained on Saipan for fiscal year 2027 budget deliberations, said he called last week’s press conference to brief the public on the delegation’s work. His chief of staff, Henry S. Hofschneider, led the 20‑member CNMI delegation.

“So this is going out to our people so they can be well informed as to how we spend the money,” Apatang said.

Hofschneider said federal officials showed strong interest in the Commonwealth’s challenges.

“One of the things that I emphasized that governor wanted to emphasize to our federal partners is that we want them to understand the Commonwealth,” he said. “To understand our constraints and to identify where we can work together.”

CNMI representatives also raised concerns about federal grant structures that place small island ports in direct competition with large mainland facilities, despite major differences in scale and logistics.

Officials described the meetings as preliminary but productive, noting that any future federal support will depend on agency review, prioritization, and long‑term policy decisions.

The governor’s office said the CNMI remains committed to working with federal and regional partners to strengthen community resilience and ensure the islands’ needs are considered as defense activities expand in the Western Pacific.

item.content:encoded:
NEW DELHI — India's opposition parties marched to the Supreme Court on Monday to protest a purge of voter lists they say favors Prime Minister Narendra Modi's party, after police detained thousands of activists over the weekend in a sweeping crackdown in New Delhi.

Several opposition lawmakers and thousands of supporters marched through the capital and submitted a petition to the chief justice alleging irregularities in the nationwide revision of voter lists.

Protests led by the "Cockroach" youth movement have intensified since election authorities began the revision last year, removing more than 130 million voters from the lists. The protesters, including opposition parties, are demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.

Critics say the process is politically motivated and risks disenfranchising eligible voters. Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party and the Election Commission deny allegations of manipulation, saying the move is needed to remove duplicate and ineligible names.

Ahead of the march, authorities closed six metro stations in the capital on Monday and warned of traffic disruptions.

Opposition leader Rahul Gandhi of the Congress party described the growing protests as a fight to defend the constitution.

"We will not back down," he told reporters in New Delhi.

Gandhi, scion of India's most influential political dynasty, is seeking to turn the protests into a broader challenge to Modi.

Gandhi briefly rode through the crowd in an open bus, waving a copy of India's Constitution. Thousands of his party supporters, student activists and other protesters followed in tow. The turnout marked a sharp contrast with the weekend, when authorities briefly detained thousands, including leaders of the "Cockroach" movement and journalists, and effectively locked down much of the capital to prevent large-scale protests.

Modi has not publicly commented on the protests, but leaders of his party have dismissed them, with some calling the activists "anarchists."

Meanwhile, New Delhi police announced Monday that Jantar Mantar, a longtime site of mass protests in the capital, would no longer be a designated venue for rallies. Police said three replacement sites had been chosen.

The "Cockroach" movement earlier this year staged a sit-in at Jantar Mantar that lasted for weeks, forcing the resignation of Modi's education minister in July.

item.content:encoded:
At almost exactly the midpoint of our conversation about the fifth album made by his band, Fontaines D.C. , Grian Chatten said to me, "It's an interesting time to be a self." We'd been talking about the themes on Dopamine Chamber , which comes out on Friday, Oct. 16, and could serve as a soundtrack to the era we live in now, what Chatten calls our "glorious age of distraction."

It's also an interesting time to be a rock band in the mainstream, and that's where Fontaines D.C., which formed in 2014, definitely lives these days. The Irish quintet's next tour has them in stadiums and arenas, and the one guest on Dopamine Chamber is pop's universal "it" girl, the Spanish singer Rosalía .

The 2024 album Romance took Fontaines to another level, earning them two Grammy nominations and their best sales ever, with hits like the sweet and earnest " Favourite ." Following it up, Fontaines didn't take the easy way. Instead, they explored new sounds to create a captivating sonic travelogue that somehow connects the decadent beauty of old Europe with the narcotic ethereality of cyberspace.

Things really gel for Fontaines on Dopamine Chamber . Using vintage synthesizers and studio effects, the band builds on the hypnotic energy that has always been its calling card to make something huge and seductive and haunting. I was lucky to speak with Chatten about his evolution as a storyteller and his place within a band that's always growing, but which remains utterly true to itself.

This conversation has been edited for length and clarity. You can listen to an extended version of this interview, plus a conversation with Fontaines D.C. bassist Conor Deegan, in the audio at the top of this page, or in the NPR Music podcast .

Ann Powers, NPR: This album comes at a kind of a milestone point in the career of Fontaines. You're playing these huge venues now, and emerging as a truly superstar band at this point. I don't know how you feel about that, but I wondered if the fact that your audience has grown so much influenced the direction this album went in. I mean in a very positive way that you seem to be kind of aiming for a monumental sound to connect with this new level of your career.

Grian Chatten: You know, the fact that there is an audience that has grown and continued to listen and moves with us, I certainly feel like it's a collaboration between ourselves and our audience, if you know what I mean. It's like, through each album, we're kind of getting closer in a spaceship to this black hole or something like that.

Well, I hope you don't fall down the black hole, because then I won't be able to hear your music anymore.

Maybe you'll have already heard it, years ago.

Oh my god, you're blowing my mind. On Dopamine Chamber there's this experience of displacement that you're getting at, and you sing a little bit about [immortality], the hubris of someone who thinks they might live forever. So how does this new album relate to those themes?

I feel like I'm writing about a metaphysical place or an imagined place that represents or reflects where I think we might be headed. And I want to do it with all the trappings and all the details of the things that I find affecting in my life: things that scare me about the future and things that warm me about the past, things that kind of comfort me. I like the idea that it's almost like a spectrum. You know the Italian singer Mina ? She came through in the '60s and she maintained a career for decades after, she's still alive, and I'm really in love with her music. And that informed and kind of armed the sense of humanity that I wanted to imbue this record with.

And then on the [other] end of the spectrum is kind of a darker, more industrial … dare I say the cliche word now: dystopian. That's people like John Mouse, who, I don't know if I [should] plug him, or like Depeche Mode and New Order and like Disintegration by The Cure . I wanted the record to feel like it was a distinct place where you walked through and you felt both of these things interacting with each other so that you could kind of get a sense of what we're losing and where we might be headed towards, you know?

Well, a dystopian story is only effective if there is a strong sense of humanity. I think about a film like Under the Skin . I mean, if Scarlett Johansson isn't there in her beauty, it doesn't have the same effect. You need to have that in any dystopian [setting]. You have to have that depth of emotion, and physical sensuality to counter and be in a dynamic relationship with machines. So maybe that's what you're going for?

Bjork does it. She's got such a beautiful, emotive and human voice. To have that piercing through the industrial music on, like, Homogenic , she had it sewn up there. I really like the feeling in Ridley Scott's films. You know, they might be isolated in a vacuum in space like how many thousands of miles or light years away from planet Earth, but they're still falling in love with each other and they've got a job to do, and a mission.

I [heard] something you said about your process to Jools Holland . You said you like to write on toilet paper because it has to go in the bin, which I thought was a little bit of that Irish humour, perhaps, but also the idea for a writer to say, "I want to cling to a notion of ephemerality about my own process." Does that free you up? The idea that your lyrics, your words, your poetry moves through space and might dissolve?

I think it's going to sound painfully, incredibly Irish of me but it's very it's important for me to recognize the transience of my own ideas and my own work, particularly before I kind of actually kind of cast them in stone in the recording and put it out there, you know, into the into the astral plane. You know, I think it's important to consider the fact that each thing I write is doomed or is to be forgotten unless I decide to actually sit down and do something about it. And I think what that does — I don't know if this makes sense — but what that does to me as a writer is it builds up my confidence in myself as the generator of the ideas, as opposed to kind of becoming beholden to one lucky burst of an idea.

But then, you know, you're writing about digital spaces on this record, and there's a sense of, everything lasts forever in digital space. I wonder if that was something you were thinking about.

That very concept of everything lasting forever immediately just makes me feel sick with how meaningless that renders everything. Like, things acquire their meaning because they're ephemeral. People love each other fiercely because they know that they're going to get old and die, you know?

A thread on this record is cinema, the idea of life as a movie. But also I know you're very inspired by films. Let's just talk about "Marianne" for a minute. I know it was inspired by the Netflix version of The Talented Mr. Ripley with Andrew Scott. When you watch something like that, how do you translate it into a song?

For me, often it takes me a while to process things.

It's not like I watched the first couple of episodes and started writing things down. It kind of ruminated for a while until I realized that the feelings I wanted to express, I was kind of like, "Oh yeah, that's how I felt when I was watching that thing." And then I kind of, at least emotionally, just thought about Andrew Scott's performance and that cinematography, the lingering shots of Italy and someone running away and, I suppose, trying to replace a human soul with material possessions and a life that isn't your own. For some reason [it was] profoundly resonant for me.

I feel like decadence is a theme that connects that song with its inspiration. And I think one question that kind of runs throughout this album is, are we at the end of something, or are we at the beginning of something? The digital age is a decadent age. You know, things are ending. You know, the earth itself is threatened. And then in talking about relationships, [there's a] trickiness sometimes of your writing where I'm not sure if you're opening your arms or if you're pushing people away.

I think I just want to make people really feel things about the world that they live in. Because it's such a terrifying world at the moment, and I think a lot of human response, which is a survival mechanism, obviously — and I don't blame anyone and I do it, of course, as well — but we run away, we hide and we distract ourselves. And we're in a glorious age of distraction. And, as you said, decadence. It really feels hugely like a cusp time. But I don't know what's next necessarily.

On the new song "Tongue," you're talking about an individual's confusion, just a kind of a desperation to put yourself right. And I wonder if going into a personal place telling an almost physical story of that experience of confusion says something about our societal experience of that?

Because of the modes of expression that we experience these days, it's not always easy to know or to trust exactly how far your words are going or how much they matter. Like, we're all kind of shouting into the void until we go viral for something that doesn't necessarily represent us. The very concept of the self is being pulled apart and sold for parts. It's just an interesting time to be a self.

That's a very David Cronenberg thing to say. I know that the band created the tracks and then you and James [Ford, the producer of Dopamine Chamber ] worked together [on the lyrics and vocals]. We've been talking a lot about heavy things and big themes. I'm just curious if those themes coalesced for you once you heard the music, or if you walked in with those themes, or you gave instructions or had a conversation with your bandmates about it before they recorded the tracks.

Well, it feels like a different part of the brain, more and more so for me anyway. Almost like I allowed the music to inform itself and not try and be too conscious about what things are about on a cerebral level. We wanted to kind of get the tone right, of futuristic, but also kind of like real, like luscious strings. On "Where Is Gone," we kind of subvert a lot of the strings with this, this instrument called the therevox, which is kind of like a theremin, but there's an eerie, kind of guttural quality to [it]. And it's definitely something a little bit more dystopian, I suppose. It subverts and kind of undermines the strings. Then once that place is fully created, then I can then I can step into it and kind of write about what it's like to be there.

Since we're talking about that song, I think it's a great moment to talk about your duet partner, Rosalía. I feel a kinship between you two in terms of your ambition, your desire to make music that goes beyond the frame and connect with other elements of art.

I've always had a sneaking suspicion that there is almost like — personally, I can't speak for the rest of the band — almost like one kind of grand thing that I'm trying to say that I'm trying to impart on on the world before I, before I get old and die, you know what I mean? There's like one thing that I'll always be chasing. I've got a suspicion that her heart is similar to mine. … I mean, she's such an incredible arranger and composer and lyricist. It's just so humbling that she was into singing on something that we had arranged. It's a career high for me, for sure.

Before we part, I do want to ask you about a couple of collaborations that took place in this time between Romance and Dopamine Chamber . You contributed two tracks to the HELP(2) [benefit] record, which is a record I absolutely love. And for the track "Flags," you worked with a bunch of different people, but particularly Damon Albarn . I thought that was interesting because he might be kind of a role model for you, the way he's done his career.

item.title: U.S. restrictions on Chinese drones are hurting cash-strapped police departments
item.description: For hours, bullets tore through the home, hitting neighboring houses and cars. Inside, a man wanted by police for allegedly killing his ex-girlfriend was holed up with his new girlfriend.
item.content:encoded:
For hours, bullets tore through the home, hitting neighboring houses and cars.

Inside, a man wanted by police for allegedly killing his ex-girlfriend was holed up with his new girlfriend.

As the SWAT team prepared to enter, Kevin Fennessy with the Ocean County Sheriff's Office tried something new first. He sent in a tiny assistant: a small drone equipped with a camera.

From a safe position outside, Fennessy slowly piloted the device through a blasted-in window, while he and other officers watched on a monitor. The video, viewed by NPR, showed hallway walls and furniture riddled with bullet holes.

As it entered a back bedroom where the couple had holed up, footage showed the man's body on the floor. He had killed himself. With the drone still hovering above the macabre scene, police deployed two flash bangs into the room. The woman rushed out and surrendered.

The incident, which happened about three years ago, sticks in Fennessy's mind when he considers the value of his department's drone program, which he heads.

"No one's hurt. Everyone's safe," Fennessy says. "Forty-one times they shot out the house at us. But at the end of the day, we were able to clear the house."

New Jersey's Ocean County Sheriff's Office is one of an estimated 6,000 law enforcement agencies across the country that now have drones, used for search and rescue, fire and traffic crash investigations, and tactical response, according to the Law Enforcement Drone Association. It's an organization that advises, trains and certifies police across the country on their drone programs.

Ocean County's entire fleet is from DJI, a Chinese manufacturer of drones. LEDA estimates that about 80% to 90% of law enforcement agencies flying drones use DJI devices. China controls a vast majority of the global drone market, and it's the dominant source for the minerals and raw materials needed to build them, researchers say.

The Trump administration wants that to end. It's made several moves to bolster U.S. drone makers , including by banning many new foreign-made drones from entering the American market. Most recently, his administration announced tariffs of 15% to 100% on some foreign-made drones, making it much more expensive for agencies to buy these devices.

Critics of these moves say the American drone industry is not yet able to keep up with demand, nor can it match the high-quality and low-cost drones made in China. Law enforcement agencies that rely on these drones are getting caught up in the fight as the federal government pushes back on the dominance of Chinese technology.

"We're seeing lives being saved with the use of this technology," says Jon Beal, head of LEDA. He says the organization supports efforts to boost the American drone industry, but that reducing access to Chinese drones is not a good solution.

"What that's going to do is cancel out perfectly viable drone programs that are doing great work out there," he says. "We don't want to cut off our nose to spite our face."

Agencies pay for drone programs in various ways, including with grants and fundraising. The Ocean County Sheriff's Office uses profits from asset forfeiture and through their municipal operating budget to cover their fleet of 25 drones.

"We have to be cost-effective. And to do that, get the best product that's available to us," Ocean County Sheriff Michael Mastronardy says.

For them, that meant turning to DJI drones.

In the parking lot of the Ocean County Sheriff's Office in early August, Fennessy breaks down the costs of the equipment one of his deputies carries in his vehicle.

A camera with infrared thermal imaging: $11,499

A (very fancy) remote controller: $1,600

A RESTUBE Automatic, a flotation device that can be dropped into water for rescues by the drone: $130.99

Fennessy acknowledges this is a huge investment, but says the devices are well-used and well worth it — especially in the summertime, when Ocean County's population nearly doubles. Major events constantly pose a policing challenge for the department, and they've found that drones have helped keep an eye on big crowds.

In July, the department used a drone to drop flotation devices to two swimmers in distress, and rescuers were able to bring them to shore.

Fennessy has become passionate about drones professionally and as a hobbyist. He's done a lot of research, including into the American drone market. "All their stuff is good," he says. "I've flown almost all of them. And I like them. I do. They make good products, but probably about three times the cost" of the DJI tools.

Beal, who says his organization is "agnostic" when it comes to what drones departments use, says he thinks Chinese-made drones are "light years ahead of what our American drones are able to do."

For instance, Beal says DJI offers a drone with an impressive, high-resolution thermal camera that costs less than $10,000 right now. He says American-made drones have worse flight-time capabilities, thermal imaging and zoom. And still they usually cost between $20,000 and $50,000, depending on the type and the model.

NPR compared the cost of two drones with similar features. The DJI Matrice 400 drone retails for about $10,500. The American-made Inspired Flight IF800 TOMCAT is going for $21,000.

Ocean County is closely monitoring recent actions by the Trump administration that could limit options for updating its fleet in the future.

Agencies in other states like Florida, Texas, Mississippi and Tennessee have had to terminate their drone programs or plans for one after state lawmakers passed bans on agencies using foreign drones. Beal says some were left scrambling to find ways to pay for more expensive American alternatives when tight department budgets couldn't cover the additional costs.

And there are more federal actions in the works.

The Federal Communications Commission is considering a new rule that would reclassify drones that use tech like thermal imaging as "military grade" — effectively banning many Chinese-made drones that have this integrated technology. Ocean County and other law enforcement use thermal imaging to assist in finding lost people or pets.
